question: At the European Council working session of 21 March (EUROPE 13376/4), the Commission proposed an increase in customs duties on Russian and Belarusian cereals, oilseeds and derived products. The new tariff will be EUR 95 per tonne or an ad valorem duty of 50 %, depending on the product. The EU plans to stop these imports. In 2023, the EU imported 4.2 million tonnes of these products from Russia.

That is around 5 % of the EU’s total cereal and oilseed imports. It should be noted that import volumes increased in 2023 compared to previous years. The main aim is to redirect Russian exports to non-EU countries. Ms von der Leyen said the EU does not want Russia to earn grain revenue from the bloc.

The aim is also to prevent goods produced in occupied Ukrainian territories from being exported to the EU through Russia. The Russian representative, Mr Pescov, condemned the Commission’s announcement, adding that European consumers would suffer as a result of this measure. In view of this: 1.

Does the Commission have a 10-year impact report for such a move, bearing in mind that the EU-Russia trade war has been going on since 2014, with damaging knock-on effects also on the Greek primary sector?
Does it believe that there should be a similar ban on economic ties between the EU and all companies operating in occupied territories such as the occupied territories of Cyprus?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2024) Council Regulation (EU) 2024/16521, which entered into force on 1 July 2024, imposes tariffs on certain grain, oilseeds, derived products and peas products from Russia and Belarus. The Regulation was prepared in response to an urgent political call by Member States and Parliament.

The impact assessment analysis was included in the explanatory memorandum accompanying the Commission’s proposal2, given the need to achieve the following objectives: to prevent EU market destabilisation through any future significant redirection of Russian grain products onto the EU market; to tackle Russian exports of illegally appropriated grain produced in the territories of Ukraine, some of which has been illegally exported to the EU market deliberately mislabelled as ‘Russian'; and to prevent Russia from using revenues from exports to the EU – of both Russian and illegally appropriated Ukrainian grain products – to fund its war of aggression against Ukraine.

The envisaged increase in customs duties is not expected to negatively affect global food security as it would not affect the transit of the products concerned through the EU territory to third countries of final destination.

The Commission is not planning to impose similar measures with respect to goods originating in other territories as it has no evidence that such imports present a risk of destabilising the EU market or that exporters outside Russia and Belarus would have illegally appropriated grain produced in other territories.
